personas.summary: Not-go as written, but close. The prose is unusually strong for a first pass: the chapter is organized around a single 'master mechanism' spine, every SMILES in all 13 assets is valid and matches its name (verified with RDKit), the answer keys for all 18 surfaced questions are chemically correct, and the trouble_spots read like they were written by someone who has graded this exam. The chemistry fails in one place: the conjugate-addition nugget asserts that 'the common hydride reagents' add 1,2 to enones, which is wrong for NaBH4 — the reagent this same chapter teaches as the standard reductant — and is the reason Luche conditions exist. Beyond that one blocker, the chapter's weaknesses are structural rather than factual: the section that is explicitly billed as the master mechanism has no mechanism figure, no mechanism question, and its only mechanism video compiles into the reader as an empty-URL block whose caption is raw storyboard direction; all eleven practice_checks exist in the package but never reach the compiled reader; the IR objective and the ozonolysis objective are taught and never assessed; the hydrate is used as an explanatory device in section 3 but not defined until section 5; and the conjugate-addition section leans on enol/enolate/tautomerization that this chapter never introduces and never lists as a prerequisite. Fix the hydride claim, restore the practice checks, suppress or fill the empty video blocks, and add mechanism-level assessment, and I would assign this.

location.anchor_text: and the common hydride reagents attack the site of highest positive charge density, the carbonyl carbon, and give 1,2 products

findings.observation: The expanded and standard prose both class 'the common hydride reagents' with organolithiums and Grignards as 1,2-selective toward alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyls. This is false for sodium borohydride, which gives substantial conjugate (1,4) reduction of enones — the well-known reason Luche conditions (NaBH4/CeCl3) exist. Only LiAlH4 and bulky/hard hydride sources are reliably 1,2. The chapter compounds this by teaching NaBH4 as the default carbonyl reductant in nugget-hydride-grignard, so a student is being told the wrong thing about a reagent they have just been handed.
findings.learner_impact: Any student asked to predict the product of NaBH4 plus 2-cyclohexenone will confidently answer the allylic alcohol and be wrong; the error will be re-taught against in the alpha-substitution/enolate chapter and in any lab that runs a Luche reduction. It also undercuts the chapter's otherwise sound hard/soft selectivity story, because the one hydride reagent named is the counterexample.
findings.evidence: nugget-conjugate-addition standard text: 'strongly basic, hard organometallics (Grignard and organolithium reagents, and hydride reagents) attack the carbonyl directly'; expanded text: 'and the common hydride reagents attack the site of highest positive charge density, the carbonyl carbon, and give 1,2 products (allylic alcohols from enones)'. Question ch19-conjugate-addition-select distractor 'd' explains NaBH4 away only as 'delivers hydride, not a methyl group', so the wrong claim is never corrected at the assessment surface either.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs the hydride-plus-enone case stated correctly: hydride selectivity toward enones is reagent-dependent, with LiAlH4 largely 1,2 and NaBH4 giving significant conjugate reduction, and learners need to be told which reagent is safe to assume for each outcome rather than being given a blanket rule.

location.anchor_text: a small fraction of the aldehyde exists as its hydrate, a gem-diol, and the hydrate is oxidized exactly as a secondary alcohol would be

findings.observation: The central mechanistic explanation of section 3 (order 3) — that aqueous oxidants overshoot the aldehyde because they oxidize the hydrate — depends on the hydration equilibrium, which is not introduced until section 5, nugget-hydration-cyanohydrin (order 5). The same forward reference appears one section earlier still, in nugget-preparation (order 2, 'allow the aldehyde to hydrate and be oxidized a second time') and in its practice_check answer. The concept prerequisites for oxidation-of-aldehydes list only carbonyl-structure-and-naming, so the dependency is neither declared nor satisfied.
findings.learner_impact: A student reading in order meets 'the hydrate, a gem-diol' as an unexplained term at the exact point where it is doing all the explanatory work. They can only memorize the outcome (aqueous oxidant overshoots) instead of understanding it, which is precisely the failure mode the chapter otherwise avoids.
findings.evidence: concepts[].order: oxidation-of-aldehydes = 3, hydration-and-cyanohydrins = 5. oxidation-of-aldehydes.prerequisites = ['carbonyl-structure-and-naming'] only. nugget-preparation practice_check answer: 'Aqueous chromium(VI) conditions would let the aldehyde hydrate and be oxidized further to the acid.'
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the hydration equilibrium must be available to the learner before it is used to explain aldehyde over-oxidation, or the oxidation section needs a self-contained introduction of the gem-diol at first use; the declared prerequisites must reflect whichever ordering is chosen.

location.anchor_text: the electrons displaced into the carbonyl make an enolate, protonation gives an enol, and tautomerization delivers the saturated carbonyl compound

findings.observation: Three ideas the chapter's own learning objective depends on — enolate, enol, and keto-enol tautomerization — are used as known vocabulary and are introduced nowhere in this chapter, nor listed in any concept's prerequisites. The same pattern recurs in nugget-imines-enamines, which invokes 'reductive amination' as a familiar reaction and forward-references the enamine alpha carbon 'in later chapters', and in nugget-preparation, whose prose assumes alcohol oxidation levels, ozonolysis, Markovnikov/anti-Markovnikov alkyne hydration, and Friedel-Crafts acylation. Every concepts[].prerequisites array in this package contains only within-chapter slugs; no cross-chapter dependency is recorded anywhere.
findings.learner_impact: The stated objective 'Draw the ketone product of a conjugate addition after tautomerization' is unachievable from this chapter alone. A student who has not yet had the enol/enolate chapter cannot follow the 1,4 pathway past the first arrow, and an instructor scheduling the chapter has no machine-readable signal of what must precede it.
findings.evidence: nugget-conjugate-addition learning_objectives includes 'Draw the ketone product of a conjugate addition after tautomerization'; the term tautomerization is used four times across the package and defined zero times. nugget-imines-enamines: 'the same balancing act reappears wherever amines and carbonyls meet, from reductive amination to enzyme active sites.' All 11 concepts' prerequisites reference only aldehydes-and-ketones slugs.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs its assumed cross-chapter prior knowledge made explicit and satisfied — either by declaring the external prerequisites so sequencing tools can enforce them, or by giving enol/enolate/tautomerization a brief in-chapter treatment sufficient to support the 1,4 objective.

location.anchor_text: Draw the general mechanism of nucleophilic addition under basic and acidic conditions.

findings.observation: The chapter's flagship objective asks students to draw the general nucleophilic addition mechanism under both basic and acidic conditions. Nothing in the chapter shows that mechanism and nothing assesses it. The two questions tagged to this concept are a reactivity ranking and a claim-evidence-reasoning item about relative rates; neither requires a single arrow. The two assets attached to the section (mol-acetone, mol-benzaldehyde) are static structures of starting materials. The one artifact that would have carried it, video-nucleophilic-addition, has production_status 'deferred'. Across all 36 compiled questions there is no mechanism, arrow-pushing, or intermediate-identification item, and no chapter figure depicts the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
findings.learner_impact: The single idea the chapter says organizes everything else is delivered only as continuous prose. Students who can recite that 'the pi electrons shift onto oxygen' have no way to practice or be checked on producing that representation, and the mechanistic 'why' the chapter builds — acid-first versus nucleophile-first — is never made retrievable.
findings.evidence: nugget-nucleophilic-addition.learning_objectives[0]; asset_ids = ['mol-acetone','mol-benzaldehyde']; video_briefs[0].production_status = 'deferred'; compiled/question-set.json counts.by_type contains no mechanism type, and both questions with concept_slug 'nucleophilic-addition-mechanism' are rank_order and structured_reasoning.
findings.recommended_outcome: The master mechanism needs a representation the learner can see step by step and an assessment that requires them to reproduce or reason over the intermediate and the electron flow, rather than only over rate comparisons.

location.anchor_text: Protonation of the hemiacetal hydroxyl converts it to a good leaving group; water departs to give an oxocarbenium ion

findings.observation: No section of the chapter contains a worked example. Every one of the eleven nuggets is continuous expository prose followed by a single practice_check that states a prompt and its answer with no intermediate steps. Multi-step sequences that students demonstrably fail on — acetal formation and hydrolysis (five discrete steps described in one paragraph), the carbinolamine-to-iminium-to-imine/enamine branch, and the protect-react-deprotect synthesis plan — are narrated at speed and never modeled.
findings.learner_impact: Students see finished reasoning but never the reasoning being performed, so they have no template for the intermediate steps. The gap is sharpest for the protecting-group workflow, where the chapter's own error_repair question (ch19-acetal-base-error) asks students to diagnose a step-order/conditions error in a synthesis they have never been walked through.
findings.evidence: nuggets[].text has only terse/standard/expanded prose variants; no nugget carries a worked_example field or a step-numbered passage. nugget-acetals expanded paragraph 2 compresses protonation, loss of water, oxocarbenium formation, second alcohol attack, and deprotection into four sentences.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs at least one fully modeled multi-step example per mechanism-heavy section — reasoning shown as it is performed, not summarized — with the acetal protect/deprotect sequence as the highest priority.

location.anchor_text: Classify 2-hexanone and hexanal as aldehyde or ketone, and state which carbon is C1 in each name.

findings.observation: All eleven nuggets carry a practice_check with a prompt and answer, but none of them appear in the compiled reader chapter. Every section in frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/aldehydes-and-ketones.json contains only text, molecule, video, mcmurry_link, and external_link blocks. The compiler emits no practice block type, so the authored retrieval practice is silently dropped between the package and the surface a student actually reads.
findings.learner_impact: A student working through the reader gets eleven sections of continuous prose with zero opportunity to self-test. The question bank exists but is a separate artifact (and is itself marked available: false), so nothing interrupts passive reading at the point of learning — the condition under which students most reliably overestimate their understanding.
findings.evidence: Every nuggets[].practice_check in topic.package.json (11 of 11); compiled reader block_type values are exclusively text/molecule/video/mcmurry_link/external_link across all 11 sections; grep for the practice_check prompt text returns no match in the reader JSON.
findings.recommended_outcome: The authored practice checks need to reach the reader surface so learners encounter retrieval at the end of each section, or the compile step needs to fail loudly when authored practice has no destination block.

location.anchor_text: Open on a ketone with the C=O polarization marked: partial positive on carbon, partial negative on oxygen.

findings.observation: All three video briefs are production_status 'deferred', yet the compiler still emits a video block into three reader sections (nucleophilic addition, acetals, Wittig). Each block has "url": "" and a description that is the verbatim first line of the storyboard — internal production direction addressed to a film crew, not to a student. There is no substitute content and no note explaining the absence.
findings.learner_impact: Students hit three broken or empty media slots at exactly the three most mechanism-dense points in the chapter, and read stage directions ('Open on the ylide: positive phosphorus adjacent to a carbanion carbon') as if they were instructional text. This reads as an unfinished product and erodes trust in the rest of the chapter.
findings.evidence: Reader sections nugget-nucleophilic-addition, nugget-acetals, nugget-wittig each contain a block with block_type 'video', content.url '' and content.description equal to video_briefs[].storyboard[0]. video_briefs[*].production_status = 'deferred' with production_note 'The reader carries the same content in the linked nugget prose and molecule figures.'
findings.recommended_outcome: Deferred video briefs must not surface to learners as empty players with storyboard text; the reader needs either the equivalent content in a form that exists, or the block suppressed until the video does.

location.anchor_text: Assign C=O IR stretches for aldehydes, ketones, and conjugated carbonyls.

findings.observation: The spectroscopy section teaches a substantial and correct body of IR content (1730 aldehyde, 1715 ketone, ~30 cm-1 conjugation shift, the diagnostic 2720/2820 aldehyde C-H pair, ring-strain effects) and states it as a learning objective, but the concept has exactly one question in the bank — ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift — which asks for a single 1H chemical shift number. No question touches IR at all; no question touches 13C. The section's only asset is a static structure of acetaldehyde; there is no spectrum figure of any kind, in a chapter whose stated selling point is that these compounds are 'the easiest functional groups to spot spectroscopically'.
findings.learner_impact: The most decision-useful skill in the section — reading conjugation off a C=O frequency, and using the 2720 cm-1 band to call aldehyde versus ketone — is taught and never practiced. The single question that exists rewards memorizing '9.7' rather than interpreting a spectrum, so students arrive at an unknown-identification exam having never been asked to do the task.
findings.evidence: nugget-carbonyl-spectroscopy.learning_objectives = ['Assign C=O IR stretches for aldehydes, ketones, and conjugated carbonyls.', 'Identify the diagnostic 1H and 13C NMR signatures of the two families.']; the only question with concept_slug 'spectroscopy-of-aldehydes-and-ketones' is ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift (numeric_with_units, value 9.7). The section's practice_check does exercise the IR reasoning but does not reach the reader (see instr-006).
findings.recommended_outcome: The IR and 13C objectives need assessment that requires interpreting actual band positions and shifts, and the section needs a spectral representation students can read rather than a table of numbers embedded in prose.

location.anchor_text: The test is named after a nineteenth-century German chemist.

findings.observation: The oxidation-of-aldehydes concept has a single question, and it is pure name recall: 'Name the classical laboratory test...'. Its level-1 hint is a biographical clue about a nineteenth-century German chemist, which rewards trivia rather than chemistry. The concept's first stated objective — explain why aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylic acids while ketones are inert — is never assessed. ch19-wittig-byproduct has the same shape (name the phosphorus byproduct), giving the chapter two of eighteen surfaced items that test vocabulary rather than reasoning.
findings.learner_impact: Students can score full marks on the oxidation concept without knowing that the aldehyde C-H is what makes the difference, which is the single idea the section is built on. It also signals to students that recall is what will be assessed, which changes how they read the rest of the chapter.
findings.evidence: ch19-tollens-test (short_answer, answer_key.answer_text lists seven spellings of 'Tollens'); its hint level 1 = 'The test is named after a nineteenth-century German chemist.' nugget-aldehyde-oxidation.learning_objectives[0] = 'Explain why aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylic acids while ketones are inert to mild oxidants.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The oxidation concept needs at least one item that makes students use the structural reason (presence or absence of the carbonyl C-H) to predict an outcome, so the concept is assessed at the level its objective states.

location.anchor_text: Ozonolysis of an alkene followed by a reductive workup (Zn/CH3COOH or dimethyl sulfide) cleaves the double bond completely

findings.observation: Ozonolysis is named in a learning objective ('Predict the carbonyl products of alkene ozonolysis and alkyne hydration'), described correctly in two sentences of prose, and then never instantiated: there is no example substrate, no figure showing a specific alkene cleaving to its two carbonyl fragments, and no question in the bank involves ozonolysis. Both preparation questions (ch19-prep-matching, ch19-ketone-routes) cover alcohol oxidation, Friedel-Crafts, and the two alkyne hydrations only.
findings.learner_impact: Ozonolysis is the one preparation in this section where students must track which alkene carbon becomes which carbonyl compound, and it is the one they get no practice on. A stated objective is unassessed and unexemplified, so students will not know it was expected of them.
findings.evidence: nugget-preparation.learning_objectives[1]; asset_ids for the section = ['mol-cyclohexanone'] only; ch19-prep-matching left items are 1-hexanol/PCC, cyclohexanol/CrO3, benzene/CH3COCl, 1-hexyne/HgSO4; ch19-ketone-routes options a-e contain no ozonolysis.
findings.recommended_outcome: Ozonolysis needs a concrete substrate-to-products instance the learner can see, plus practice that requires mapping each alkene carbon to its carbonyl product, matching the level of the stated objective.

location.anchor_text: A secondary alcohol, 1-phenylethanol — the direct product is the magnesium alkoxide

findings.observation: The chapter never addresses the stereochemical consequence of nucleophilic addition. A planar sp2 carbonyl is attacked with equal probability from either face, so addition to a prochiral carbonyl gives a racemic mixture. The chapter's own flagship example — CH3MgBr plus benzaldehyde giving 1-phenylethanol — creates a stereocenter, and neither the prose, the practice_check answer, the asset mol-1-phenylethanol (SMILES CC(O)c1ccccc1, no stereodescriptor and no note), nor question ch19-grignard-product mentions that the product is racemic. The nucleophilic-addition nugget describes the trigonal-to-tetrahedral rehybridization in detail without ever noting that this is where the stereocenter is born.
findings.learner_impact: Students coming out of the stereochemistry chapters are primed to ask about this and get no answer; worse, drawing a single enantiomer of 1-phenylethanol as 'the product' teaches an incorrect model that will need un-teaching in any later treatment of asymmetric reduction or enzymatic ketone reduction.
findings.evidence: assets mol-1-phenylethanol smiles 'CC(O)c1ccccc1' with alt_text 'a carbon that bears a hydroxyl group, a methyl group, and one hydrogen — a secondary alcohol' (no stereochemistry mentioned); nugget-hydride-grignard practice_check answer names 1-phenylethanol with no stereochemical comment; ch19-grignard-product option a same SMILES, no stereo.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs the facial-attack consequence made explicit at the point a stereocenter is first formed — that addition to a planar carbonyl gives both enantiomers in equal amounts — so the flat structures shown are correctly interpreted.

location.anchor_text: Ammonia and amines are good nucleophiles, and their addition to aldehydes and ketones opens a family of condensation products

findings.observation: The nitrogen-nucleophile section opens by promising 'a family of condensation products' and then delivers exactly two members: the alkylamine imine and the secondary-amine enamine. The substituted-hydrazine and hydroxylamine derivatives that constitute the rest of that family in every standard treatment of this chapter — oximes, hydrazones, semicarbazones — are absent, as is Wolff-Kishner reduction, which is the reason hydrazone formation is taught at all and the chapter's only route from C=O to CH2. Baeyer-Villiger oxidation is likewise absent from the oxidation section, which asserts that 'only forcing conditions that break carbon-carbon bonds can degrade' ketones without naming the standard method that does so.
findings.learner_impact: Students assigned this chapter alongside a standard textbook will find a visible content gap; more importantly, they leave without the C=O to CH2 transformation, so their retrosynthetic toolkit has a hole exactly where Friedel-Crafts acylation (taught in this chapter's preparation section) creates the need for it.
findings.evidence: nugget-imines-enamines covers only imine and enamine; ch19-amine-outcomes uses methylamine, dimethylamine, aniline, pyrrolidine — all C- or H-substituted amines, no N- or O-substituted nucleophiles. nugget-aldehyde-oxidation: 'only forcing conditions that break carbon-carbon bonds can degrade them.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs a decision about scope made deliberately and stated: either the remaining nitrogen-nucleophile condensations and the C=O to CH2 deoxygenation belong here, or their absence needs to be flagged so instructors know to supply them.

location.anchor_text: Select the correct IUPAC name for the compound shown: CH₃COCH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃.

findings.observation: The distractor structures undermine the question. Option b ('2-Methyl-4-pentanone') carries structure_smiles 'CC(=O)CC(C)C' — byte-identical to correct option a — so if the surface renders option structures the student sees two identical drawings under different names. Meanwhile options c and d carry structures that do not match the stem compound at all (an alcohol, C6H14O; and 2-methylpentanal), so a student who ignores the names entirely can eliminate c and d on structure alone and face a coin flip. The stem itself is given only as a condensed formula with no rendered structure, so the option structures are the only drawings in the item.
findings.learner_impact: The item no longer measures naming skill: it can be reduced to a two-way guess by structure-matching, and the duplicated render is actively confusing for students who do read carefully. A student who selects b and reads the (correct) feedback about numbering will still be looking at a picture identical to the right answer's.
findings.evidence: ch19-iupac-name.student_config.options: a text '4-Methyl-2-pentanone' smiles 'CC(=O)CC(C)C'; b text '2-Methyl-4-pentanone' smiles 'CC(=O)CC(C)C'; c 'CC(O)CC(C)C'; d 'CCCC(C)C=O'. RDKit confirms a and b are the same molecule and c, d are different molecules from the stem.
findings.recommended_outcome: The naming item needs its stimulus and its options to carry consistent structural information — one authoritative structure for the stem, and options that cannot be resolved by structure-matching instead of by naming rules.

location.anchor_text: The compromise, mildly acidic solution, keeps a workable fraction of both reactive species present

findings.observation: The pH 4.5 optimum is correct and the trade-off is correctly identified, but the stated reason invites a wrong quantitative model. At pH 4.5 a typical primary alkylamine (conjugate acid pKa around 10.6) is more than 99.99% protonated — the free-amine fraction is roughly 10^-6, not 'a workable fraction'. The reaction is fast there because the rate is the product of a tiny free-amine concentration and a greatly accelerated dehydration, not because both species are appreciably present. No pKa value appears anywhere in the chapter to let a student check this.
findings.learner_impact: Students who accept 'both species present in workable amounts' will predict, wrongly, that the free-amine concentration is appreciable at pH 4.5, and will be unable to reconcile the chapter's claim with an amine pKa table they can look up. It also sets them up to mis-reason about every other rate-versus-speciation problem (enzyme pH optima, buffer selection).
findings.evidence: nugget-imines-enamines expanded paragraph 3; ch19-imine-ph-optimum answer_key value 4.5 tolerance 0.5, and its wrong_answer_explanation for pH 2 ('still acidic enough to protonate most of the amine') implies that at 4.5 most of the amine is not protonated. No pKa or pKaH value appears in any nugget in the package.
findings.recommended_outcome: The pH-optimum explanation needs to be grounded in the actual speciation — a stated amine pKaH and the recognition that the optimum is a rate product, not a point where both species are abundant — so the correct mechanism reasoning is not bought with a false quantitative picture.

location.anchor_text: attacks that carbon along a trajectory roughly 105° to the C=O axis

findings.observation: All 13 assets in this chapter are type 'molecule' — static structures of starting materials and products. Nothing in the chapter's visual layer carries a process: not the Burgi-Dunitz approach angle and sp2-to-sp3 rehybridization described in the prose above, not the aldehyde-versus-ketone transition-state energy comparison that the whole reactivity argument rests on, not the reversible acetal equilibrium whose direction is controlled by water, and not the 1,2-versus-1,4 branch point. Peer packages in this same content set do carry process figures (11 reaction_coordinate assets, plus conformational_energy_profile, newman_projection, and synthesis_roadmap types across other chapters); this chapter uses none of them.
findings.learner_impact: Every dynamic idea in the chapter — trajectory, rehybridization, transition-state crowding, equilibrium direction, competing pathways — is available to the student only as a sentence to be parsed. The reactivity ordering in particular is asserted verbally and then tested by ch19-reactivity-ranking, so students must hold a four-way steric/electronic comparison entirely in prose.
findings.evidence: assets[] in topic.package.json: 13 entries, all type 'molecule'. Across all topic packages: molecule 241, reaction_coordinate 11, stereochemistry_conversion 3, conformational_energy_profile 3, synthesis_roadmap 1, newman_projection 1 — none of the non-molecule types appear in aldehydes-and-ketones.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs representations that show change rather than end states — at minimum for the aldehyde-versus-ketone transition-state comparison and the 1,2/1,4 branch point, where the teaching claim is about relative energies and competing pathways that a static structure cannot convey.

location.anchor_text: NaBH4 is mild, selective for aldehydes and ketones, and tolerant of protic solvents; LiAlH4 is far stronger

findings.observation: Coverage across concepts is uneven. hydride-and-grignard-addition and conjugate-addition carry one question each, while carbonyl-structure-and-naming, preparation, hydration, imines, acetals, and wittig carry two. The single hydride/Grignard item (ch19-grignard-product) is a core-difficulty product-identification select; the reagent-selection judgment the section actually teaches — NaBH4 versus LiAlH4, and why an ester survives one and not the other — is never assessed, nor is the second stated objective about the separate aqueous workup. Additionally, all 36 compiled questions have demo_eligible false, so none of this bank is surfaced in the demo path.
findings.learner_impact: The reagent-choice decision is the transferable skill in this section and the one students carry into synthesis problems; it is taught and left untested. An instructor pulling from this bank cannot build a balanced quiz without writing new hydride items themselves.
findings.evidence: compiled/question-set.json counts: 36 questions, 18 surfaced, demo_eligible 0. Questions by concept_slug: hydride-and-grignard-addition = ch19-grignard-product (+v2) only; conjugate-addition = ch19-conjugate-addition-select (+v2) only. nugget-hydride-grignard.learning_objectives[1] = 'Explain why an aqueous workup is a separate, necessary step.'
findings.recommended_outcome: Assessment needs to reach the reagent-selection and workup-necessity judgments in the hydride/Grignard section, and coverage across the eleven concepts needs to be levelled so no core concept rests on a single recognition item.

location.anchor_text: 4-Methylpentan-2-ol

findings.observation: Nomenclature style is mixed within single option lists and across the chapter. ch19-iupac-name offers '4-Methyl-2-pentanone' (substituent-prefix style) alongside '4-Methylpentan-2-ol' (locant-in-name style) as parallel choices. The prose likewise mixes '2-cyclohexenone' with '1-methyl-2-cyclohexen-1-ol' and '3-methylcyclohexanone'. Separately, Greek letters are spelled out throughout the prose ('alpha,beta-unsaturated', 'the alpha carbon') while other symbols are set as Unicode (π, σ, sp², cm⁻¹, ¹H, ¹³C), and 'lithium aluminium hydride' / 'aluminium chloride' use British spelling against otherwise US-convention text.
findings.learner_impact: In a naming question specifically, presenting two different naming conventions as parallel options adds noise to the discrimination the item is trying to measure; students may read the style difference as the thing being tested. Elsewhere the inconsistency is cosmetic but signals uneven authoring.
findings.evidence: ch19-iupac-name options a ('4-Methyl-2-pentanone') and c ('4-Methylpentan-2-ol'); nugget-conjugate-addition expanded: '1-methyl-2-cyclohexen-1-ol' and '3-methylcyclohexanone'; nugget-hydride-grignard: 'lithium aluminium hydride'; nugget-conjugate-addition title uses 'alpha,beta-unsaturated' while the same package uses π and sp² as Unicode.
findings.recommended_outcome: One nomenclature convention and one symbol convention need to hold across prose, figures, and question options, especially inside a naming item where the convention is not the construct being assessed.

location.anchor_text: attacks that carbon along a trajectory roughly 105° to the C=O axis

findings.observation: The nucleophile approach angle is given twice (prose and the video-nucleophilic-addition storyboard) as 'roughly 105° to the C=O axis'. The commonly cited Burgi-Dunitz value is about 107°, the angle is never named, and 'to the C=O axis' is ambiguous about what it is measured from. Nothing in the chapter depicts the angle, so a student has a bare number with no anchor.
findings.learner_impact: A precise-looking number with no name, no reference geometry, and no picture is memorization bait: students will record '105 degrees' without understanding that it encodes approach along the pi* lobe, which is the only reason the number is interesting.
findings.evidence: nugget-nucleophilic-addition expanded text and video_briefs[0].storyboard[1] both state 'roughly 105° to the C=O axis'; the term Burgi-Dunitz appears nowhere in the package; no asset depicts the trajectory.
findings.recommended_outcome: The approach angle needs to be either named and geometrically anchored so the number means something, or dropped in favour of the qualitative claim about attack perpendicular to the carbonyl plane.

location.anchor_text: "difficulty": "core"

findings.observation: All eleven concepts are marked difficulty 'core' and none carries a teacher_optional flag or why_optional note, totalling 70 minutes of nugget content covering naming, four preparation routes, oxidation, the general mechanism, six distinct addition reactions, and spectroscopy. Peer packages in this set (acids-bases-and-curved-arrows, alkenes-reactions-and-synthesis) do use teacher_optional/why_optional to mark reducible scope.
findings.learner_impact: An instructor with fewer contact hours has no authored guidance about what can be dropped, and a struggling student has no signal about which of eleven equally-weighted sections carry the load-bearing ideas. The chapter's own structure identifies nucleophilic-addition-mechanism as the spine, but the metadata does not.
findings.evidence: concepts[] all have difficulty 'core'; no concept has teacher_optional or why_optional keys, which do appear in acids-bases-and-curved-arrows and alkenes-reactions-and-synthesis. Sum of nuggets[].duration_minutes = 70.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs its reducible scope marked so instructors can shorten it deliberately and students can see which sections the rest depend on.

location.anchor_text: it is made by oxidizing cyclohexanol and undergoes every addition in the chapter — hydride, Grignard, amine, alcohol, and ylide

findings.observation: The mol-cyclohexanone asset declares concept_slugs ['preparation-of-aldehydes-and-ketones', 'nucleophilic-addition-mechanism'] but nugget_ids ['nugget-preparation'] only, so the compiler places it in the preparation section alone. Its learning_goal explicitly frames it as the chapter's workhorse substrate for every addition, and cyclohexanone is in fact the substrate for the imine, enamine, acetal, and Wittig examples — but the figure never appears alongside any of them.
findings.learner_impact: The recurring-substrate thread the asset is written to carry is invisible to the reader: four later sections discuss cyclohexanone derivatives with no anchor structure of cyclohexanone itself in view, so the deliberate reuse that would reduce cognitive load is lost.
findings.evidence: assets mol-cyclohexanone concept_slugs vs nugget_ids mismatch; compiled reader places the cyclohexanone molecule block only in section nugget-preparation, while nugget-imines-enamines, nugget-acetals, and nugget-wittig show only cyclohexanone-derived products.
findings.recommended_outcome: The recurring-substrate figure needs to be present wherever the chapter reasons from it, so the intended thread through the addition sections is actually visible to the reader.

strengths: Every SMILES in the package is valid and matches its stated compound name — verified with RDKit across all 13 assets, all option-level structure_smiles, and both structure_scaffold answer keys (13/13 assets, 21/21 structures checked).

All 18 surfaced answer keys are chemically correct, including the regiochemically delicate ones: mercury-catalyzed versus hydroboration alkyne hydration in ch19-prep-matching and ch19-ketone-routes, the aniline-gives-imine case in ch19-amine-outcomes, and the cuprate 1,4 selectivity in ch19-conjugate-addition-select.

The chapter is genuinely organized around one mechanism rather than a list of reactions: nine of eleven concepts declare nucleophilic-addition-mechanism as prerequisite, and each reaction section is written as that mechanism with a different nucleophile.

The concepts[].trouble_spots are unusually well-observed — the PCC-versus-aqueous-chromium overshoot, the imine-versus-enamine N-H count, and the 'ketones are bigger so they must be more reactive' inversion are exactly the errors that recur on exams.

Explanations reach for mechanism rather than assertion in most places: aldehyde over-oxidation is explained through the hydrate, acetal robustness through the absence of a leaving group without protonation, and the Wittig's positional certainty is contrasted against Zaitsev dehydration with a specific worked contrast (methylenecyclohexane versus 1-methylcyclohexene).

Wrong-answer explanations are specific and diagnostic rather than generic — ch19-grignard-product's four distractor explanations each name the precise misconception (chain extension at the wrong carbon, addition versus substitution, hydride versus carbon nucleophile).

Distractor design in ch19-aldehyde-vs-ketone-reasoning is strong: it includes one plausible non-evidence option (molecular mass and diffusion) that forces students to distinguish evidence from irrelevant true statements.

Every question ships a hint ladder and an accessible_description, and the structure_scaffold items correctly choose achiral products (acetone cyanohydrin, methylenecyclohexane) so a single-SMILES answer key is unambiguous.

I do not agree that static product structures carry the electron flow of a mechanism, but I flag it as a question because the deferral appears to be a standing pipeline decision (chapters 12-18) rather than a choice made for this chapter.

personas.summary: The prose is clear, well-organized, and unusually consistent in its central idea (polarized C=O → nucleophile attacks carbon), and the question bank's hint ladders and wrong-answer explanations are genuinely good. But as a reader experience for a shaky student this chapter is prose-plus-static-structures and almost nothing else: the compiled reader ships 11 expanded-prose blocks, 17 single-molecule pictures, 11 Wikipedia links, and three video blocks that are emitted with url:"" and is_hidden:true, so they render as nothing. Every mechanism in a chapter titled "Nucleophilic Addition Reactions" — the tetrahedral alkoxide, carbinolamine, iminium, oxocarbenium, oxaphosphetane, enolate — is named in sentences but never drawn anywhere in the package. The nuggets' practice_check prompts and learning_objectives exist in the source but are not compiled into the reader, and the question set is available:false with demo_eligible:0, so a student reading the chapter has zero checkpoints, zero worked examples, and zero retrieval practice between the opening sentence and the end. Several terms I would stall on (alpha carbon, the 1/4 counting in "1,4 addition", hard vs. soft nucleophiles, thermodynamic control, the 105° trajectory) are used at first appearance with no setup. I would finish this chapter able to recite the sentences and unable to do a single problem.

location.anchor_text: the π electrons shift entirely onto oxygen, the carbon rehybridizes from sp² to sp³, and the product is a tetrahedral alkoxide

findings.observation: The chapter's declared master mechanism has no depiction of the electron flow anywhere a student can see it. The only assets in this section are two static single-molecule renderings (mol-acetone, mol-benzaldehyde) of starting materials; the one mechanism animation (video-nucleophilic-addition) is compiled into the reader as block blk-r8gcfq5b with "url": "" and "is_hidden": true, and ReaderBlockRenderer returns null for hidden blocks. The tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate itself is never drawn.
findings.learner_impact: A student who cannot yet convert 'π electrons shift onto oxygen' into a picture has nothing to check their mental model against. I would reread the paragraph two or three times, decide I 'get it,' and then be unable to draw the intermediate on the first practice problem — the classic point where I stop reading and go look for a YouTube video instead.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets[] contains 14 entries, all type 'molecule' single structures; reader chapter section nugget-nucleophilic-addition blocks = text, molecule, molecule, video(url empty, is_hidden true), external_link.
findings.recommended_outcome: The step-by-step electron flow of the general nucleophilic addition — attack, π shift, tetrahedral alkoxide, protonation — needs to exist in a form a reader actually receives, not only as sentences and a suppressed video block.

location.anchor_text: the product is a carbinolamine — a tetrahedral intermediate with OH and NR₂ on the same carbon

findings.observation: Four named intermediates carry the multi-step condensations — carbinolamine, iminium ion, oxocarbenium ion, oxaphosphetane — and none of them is drawn in any asset. The assets for these sections show only the final products (mol-cyclohexanone-methylimine, mol-cyclohexanone-pyrrolidine-enamine, mol-cyclohexanone-ethylene-acetal, mol-methylenecyclohexane).
findings.learner_impact: I have to hold an unseen structure in working memory across a five-step sentence ('protonation of the hydroxyl converts it into water, which leaves to give a resonance-stabilized iminium ion; deprotonation of the nitrogen then delivers the imine'). I would guess at the intermediates, and I would very likely produce the enamine when asked for the imine because I never saw where the proton came off.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets[] — no asset for any intermediate; nugget-acetals text 'water departs to give an oxocarbenium ion stabilized by the remaining alkoxy oxygen'; nugget-wittig text 'forming a four-membered ring called an oxaphosphetane'.
findings.recommended_outcome: Students need the intermediates of imine, enamine, acetal, and Wittig formation made visible at each stage, not only the start and end structures.

location.anchor_text: practice_check

findings.observation: Every one of the 11 nuggets authors a practice_check {prompt, answer}, but the compiled reader contains no practice block of any kind: the block_type census for aldehydes-and-ketones.json is 11 text, 17 molecule, 11 external_link, 1 mcmurry_link, 3 video (all hidden). The separate question set is compiled with "available": false and "demo_eligible": 0.
findings.learner_impact: A reader gets eleven straight blocks of exposition with no checkpoint. With weak prerequisites I cannot tell whether I have understood section 4 before section 5 assumes it; I read passively to the end, feel vaguely fine, and discover on the exam that none of it stuck.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nuggets[].practice_check present for all 11 nuggets; compiled/question-set.json counts: {questions: 36, surfaced: 18, demo_eligible: 0}, available: false.
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs an in-place way for a reader to test recall at the end of each section rather than having all retrieval practice held in an unavailable bank.

location.anchor_text: a proton is removed from the adjacent alpha carbon instead

findings.observation: 'Alpha carbon' is used for the first time in this nugget and is never defined anywhere in the chapter. It then recurs as load-bearing vocabulary in nugget-carbonyl-spectroscopy ('protons on the alpha carbons ... 2.0–2.6 ppm'), in nugget-conjugate-addition, and in the distractor of question ch19-conjugate-addition-select-v2 ('The alpha carbon, between the two π systems'). Nugget-carbonyl-structure-naming, which teaches numbering, never introduces the alpha/beta labeling system.
findings.learner_impact: I do not know whether alpha means C1 or the carbon next to the carbonyl, so the enamine explanation becomes 'a proton comes off some carbon.' On ch19-conjugate-addition-select-v2 I would pick the alpha-carbon distractor because it is described as sitting 'between the two π systems,' which sounds like the activated position.
findings.evidence: Search of all 11 nuggets: 'alpha carbon' first appears in nugget-imines-enamines standard text with no definition; 'beta carbon' is only loosely glossed in nugget-conjugate-addition as 'two atoms away'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The alpha/beta position labels relative to a carbonyl need to be established before the first section that reasons with them.

location.anchor_text: Direct addition at the carbonyl carbon is called 1,2 addition

findings.observation: The 1,2 / 1,4 numbering is used throughout the section (and in two question prompts) but the chapter never says what atoms 1 and 4 are — that the count starts at the carbonyl oxygen. The nearest thing to an explanation is 'bonds the nucleophile to the beta carbon; ... two atoms away', which uses a different counting origin than the 1,4 label does.
findings.learner_impact: Two incompatible numbering schemes in one paragraph is exactly where I stop and try to memorize the labels as arbitrary names. I would then be unable to answer 'which carbon does the nitrogen attack' (ch19-conjugate-addition-select-v2) by reasoning, and would guess from reagent recall alone.
findings.evidence: nugget-conjugate-addition expanded text; question ch19-conjugate-addition-select prompt 'delivers its methyl group to the beta carbon (conjugate, 1,4 addition)'.
findings.recommended_outcome: Students need the 1,2 versus 1,4 labels tied explicitly to positions counted from the carbonyl oxygen, reconciled with the alpha/beta labels used in the same paragraph.

location.anchor_text: Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration in aqueous sulfuric acid places the hydroxyl on the internal carbon (Markovnikov), and the resulting enol tautomerizes to a methyl ketone.

findings.observation: One 7-minute 'core' nugget carries six distinct preparations (PCC/Dess–Martin, aqueous Cr(VI), ozonolysis with reductive workup, Hg(II) hydration, hydroboration–oxidation, Friedel–Crafts acylation) and silently reuses at least five prior-chapter concepts as known: Markovnikov/anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry, enol tautomerization, reductive workup, hindered borane, and the acylium electrophile. The section's only figure is mol-cyclohexanone, a single product structure. The concept record preparation-of-aldehydes-and-ketones lists only one prerequisite, carbonyl-structure-and-naming — none of the alkene/alkyne/aromatic chemistry it actually depends on.
findings.learner_impact: This is the point where a student with weak prerequisites quits and starts making a flashcard deck of reagent→product pairs, which is precisely the memorization the rest of the chapter is designed to avoid. Nothing signals that this section is a review of old material rather than new theory.
findings.evidence: nugget-preparation standard and expanded text; concepts[].prerequisites for preparation-of-aldehydes-and-ketones = ['carbonyl-structure-and-naming']; asset_ids = ['mol-cyclohexanone'].
findings.recommended_outcome: This section needs its prior-chapter dependencies named up front and its six transformations chunked or visually contrasted, so a shaky student can tell what is review and where to go refresh.

location.anchor_text: Nearly every reaction of an aldehyde or ketone follows the same two-step pattern, which makes this the most economical mechanism in the course to learn well.

findings.observation: The unifying mechanism is section 4 of 11, placed after 'Where aldehydes and ketones come from' (six memorization-heavy preparations) and 'Aldehydes oxidize easily'. The two sections that precede it are the most prerequisite-dependent in the chapter and gain nothing from being read first.
findings.learner_impact: I spend my freshest attention on a reagent list, arrive at the actual organizing idea already tired, and never get the payoff of re-reading the earlier sections through it. Nothing in the reader tells me section 4 is the one to master.
findings.evidence: reader chapter sections order: nugget-carbonyl-structure-naming, nugget-preparation, nugget-aldehyde-oxidation, nugget-nucleophilic-addition, ...
findings.recommended_outcome: The reader needs the master mechanism to be reachable (or at least flagged as the load-bearing section) before the recall-heavy preparation material, or an explicit forward pointer telling a struggling student what to prioritize.

location.anchor_text: learning_objectives

findings.observation: Every nugget authors learning_objectives and a depth field, but neither is compiled into the reader — the reader block list per section is text + molecules + links only. All 11 nuggets are depth 'core', and the concepts[] entries all have objectives: null. There is also no chapter-opening roadmap block and no closing summary block.
findings.learner_impact: Nothing in what I actually read distinguishes 'you must be able to draw this' from 'nice to know'. With everything equally weighted I default to highlighting every sentence, which is what a low-confidence student does instead of prioritizing.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json nuggets[].learning_objectives populated (e.g. three objectives on nugget-nucleophilic-addition); compiled reader JSON contains no objective or summary block; concepts[].objectives is null for all 11 concepts.
findings.recommended_outcome: Readers need a visible signal of what each section requires them to be able to do, and a chapter-level entry/exit summary so importance is not flat.

location.anchor_text: Saturated aldehydes absorb near 1730 cm⁻¹ and saturated ketones near 1715 cm⁻¹

findings.observation: The spectroscopy section asks the student to internalize roughly ten numeric landmarks (1730, 1715, −30 shift, 2720/2820, 9–10 ppm, 2.0–2.6 ppm, 190–205, 200–215, 206, 5–10 upfield) and its only asset is mol-acetaldehyde, a static structure. No IR trace and no NMR trace exists anywhere in the package, yet questions ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift and ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift-v2 ask for numeric shifts.
findings.learner_impact: Numbers with no picture to hang them on are pure rote for me; I would confuse the 1730/1715 pair with the 2720/2820 pair within a day and I have no way to see that 'downfield of the aromatic region' is a place on an axis rather than a phrase.
findings.evidence: nugget-carbonyl-spectroscopy asset_ids = ['mol-acetaldehyde']; question ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift accessibility_bundle describes a purely numeric entry with no stimulus figure.
findings.recommended_outcome: The diagnostic IR and NMR landmarks need a spatial representation a student can point at, so the numbers are read off a picture instead of memorized as a list.

location.anchor_text: attacks that carbon along a trajectory roughly 105° to the C=O axis

findings.observation: A specific geometric fact (the Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory) is stated as a number in prose, unnamed and unillustrated, in the middle of the mechanism paragraph. Nothing tells the student whether it matters, and no figure shows an angle 'to the C=O axis'.
findings.learner_impact: I cannot picture an angle relative to an axis from a sentence, so I either try to memorize '105°' as a testable fact or skip it and lose confidence that I am reading carefully enough. Either way it costs attention that the actual mechanism needs.
findings.evidence: nugget-nucleophilic-addition expanded text, first paragraph.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the attack geometry needs a representation a student can see, or it needs to be marked as background detail so it does not compete with the mechanism steps.

location.anchor_text: Softer, more polarizable and less basic nucleophiles — primary and secondary amines, thiols, cyanide — prefer the beta carbon, where the reaction is under thermodynamic control

findings.observation: Three unexplained frameworks land in two consecutive sentences: hard/soft nucleophile character, polarizability, and thermodynamic versus kinetic control. None is defined in this chapter, none appears in the concept prerequisites (conjugate-addition lists only nucleophilic-addition-mechanism), and 'kinetic control' is never named as the contrast partner even though the 1,2 pathway is the kinetic one.
findings.learner_impact: I would reduce the whole section to the memorized pair 'cuprate = 1,4, Grignard = 1,2' and be unable to place any new nucleophile. The generic feedback on ch19-conjugate-addition-select-v2 reuses the same undefined phrase ('thermodynamically controlled outcome'), so getting it wrong does not rescue me.
findings.evidence: nugget-conjugate-addition expanded text, paragraph 2; feedback_bundle.generic_incorrect_explanation of ch19-conjugate-addition-select-v2.
findings.recommended_outcome: The hard/soft and thermodynamic-versus-kinetic ideas either need enough setup to be usable for prediction, or the selectivity rule needs a form a student can apply without them.

location.anchor_text: Predict the alcohol class formed when a hydride or Grignard reagent adds to a given carbonyl compound.

findings.observation: The chapter contains no worked example anywhere — no solved problem that shows intermediate reasoning. The closest artifacts are the practice_check answers, which are one-sentence assertions ('3-Methylcyclohexanone. The cuprate adds its methyl group 1,4 at the beta carbon'), and they are not compiled into the reader. The hydride/Grignard concept, whose stated objective is prediction across four substrate cases (formaldehyde/other aldehyde/ketone, hydride vs. carbanion), gets only two questions and both are Grignard single_selects; NaBH₄/LiAlH₄ selection is never practiced.
findings.learner_impact: The step I actually get stuck on — deciding which substituents end up on the former carbonyl carbon, and therefore which alcohol class results — is the step that is never shown being done. I would answer the multiple-choice items by pattern-matching the option labels ('a secondary alcohol') rather than by working the structure out, and then fail an open-ended version.
findings.evidence: nugget-hydride-grignard practice_check answer; question_sets: only ch19-grignard-product and ch19-grignard-product-v2 for concept hydride-and-grignard-addition, both single_select, both CH₃MgBr.
findings.recommended_outcome: Students need at least one fully worked substrate-to-product derivation for the carbonyl→alcohol classes, plus practice that covers the hydride half of the stated objective.

location.anchor_text: Base leaves acetals completely untouched

findings.observation: The chapter's common wrong moves are corrected only inside question feedback, and the question bank is available:false with demo_eligible:0, so a reader never meets them. concepts[] has no misconceptions field populated for any of the 11 concepts, and no reader block names a typical error. The traps that do get corrected (base-hydrolysis of an acetal, one equivalent of methanol, Jones overshoot, Grignard alkoxide before workup) live in ch19-acetal-base-error, ch19-acetal-base-error-v2, ch19-ketone-routes-v2, and ch19-grignard-product feedback only.
findings.learner_impact: I only discover the trap by falling into it, and right now I cannot even do that because the questions are not surfaced. Reading the prose alone, I would keep the wrong model (e.g. that 'protecting group removal' means base) all the way to an exam.
findings.evidence: concepts[] entries contain no misconceptions; compiled/question-set.json available: false, counts.demo_eligible: 0; feedback_bundle of ch19-acetal-base-error.
findings.recommended_outcome: The named common errors already identified by the question authors need to reach a reader who never opens the question bank.

location.anchor_text: Draw a central carbon bearing two methyls, an OH, and a C≡N group: CC(C)(O)C#N.

findings.observation: All four structure_scaffold items end their hint ladder with the literal answer SMILES (ch19-draw-cyanohydrin, ch19-draw-cyanohydrin-v2 'N#CC(O)c1ccccc1', ch19-draw-wittig-product 'C=C1CCCCC1', ch19-draw-wittig-product-v2 'C=Cc1ccccc1'). These are also the only four items with three hint levels; every other item stops at two conceptual hints.
findings.learner_impact: As the student most likely to open every hint, I get handed the answer at level 3 and do no drawing reasoning at all, then believe I can do these problems. The hint ladder rewards exactly the avoidance behavior I need to be pulled out of.
findings.evidence: feedback_bundle.hints level 3 of all four structure_scaffold questions.
findings.recommended_outcome: The final hint on drawing items needs to constrain the answer without supplying it, so a stuck student still performs the construction step.

location.anchor_text: With simple, unstabilized ylides the reaction favors the Z alkene where geometry is in question; stabilized ylides bearing an adjacent carbonyl group favor E.

findings.observation: Stabilized versus unstabilized ylides and their E/Z outcomes are introduced in a single sentence, with no example, no structure, and no supporting question — the two Wittig drawing items both use the same unhindered CH₂ ylide where geometry does not arise, and neither Wittig learning objective mentions alkene geometry.
findings.learner_impact: One sentence naming two reagent classes and two stereochemical outcomes reads as something I am expected to memorize, but there is no way to practice it, so it becomes anxiety rather than knowledge.
findings.evidence: nugget-wittig expanded text paragraph 3; learning_objectives of nugget-wittig; ch19-draw-wittig-product and -v2 both use Ph₃P=CH₂.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the E/Z selectivity needs enough support and practice to be learnable, or it should be marked as beyond what this chapter expects.

location.anchor_text: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbonyl group

findings.observation: The only per-section supporting resource in the reader is a Wikipedia link (11 of them, one per section), and the URLs are emitted with unencoded spaces — e.g. '/wiki/Carbonyl group', '/wiki/Tollens' reagent', '/wiki/Nucleophilic addition'. Only one McMurry/OpenStax link exists for the whole chapter, attached to section 1.
findings.learner_impact: When I am stuck in section 6 the offered help is a Wikipedia article written above my level, and the assigned-textbook link is nine sections back where I will not look for it. Malformed URLs make the one escape hatch feel unreliable.
findings.evidence: reader chapter external_link blocks, 11 total; mcmurry_link block blk-daxpjnzn appears only in nugget-carbonyl-structure-naming.
findings.recommended_outcome: Per-section escape hatches should point at level-appropriate, correctly formed targets, and the assigned-textbook reading should be reachable from any section where a student stalls.

strengths: The chapter keeps one explanatory thread — polarized C=O, nucleophile attacks carbon — and genuinely reuses it in every later section, which is exactly the kind of consistency a shaky student can hold on to.

Every question in the bank has a two-level hint ladder that moves from orientation to strategy without giving the answer (e.g. ch19-classify-carbonyls level 1 'Find the C=O carbon and look at what else is bonded to it').

Wrong-answer explanations are specific and diagnostic rather than generic — ch19-grignard-product explains each distractor structurally, and ch19-aldehyde-nmr-shift explains why 7.3 and 2.2 ppm are the wrong regions.

The error_repair items (ch19-acetal-base-error, ch19-acetal-base-error-v2) are built around real student errors and explicitly confirm the part of the flawed work that was correct, which is unusually good for confidence.
Alt text on the molecule assets describes what is on the carbonyl carbon rather than just naming the compound, which makes the static figures usable as reasoning aids.
open_questions: Three video briefs are compiled into the reader with url:"" and is_hidden:true, so they render as nothing ([internal source reference — not in this repo]). I scored the resulting mechanism gap as high rather than blocker because the prose does state every step — but if another persona treats the deferred mechanism videos as a required-access failure, this may need to escalate.

Is the reader intended to expose the terse/standard depth variants and the nugget practice_check at all? Only the expanded text is compiled today, so finding stud-003 assumes the practice prompts are genuinely unreachable rather than pending a renderer feature.

The question set is compiled with available:false and demo_eligible:0. Several of my findings (retrieval practice, named misconceptions) would soften considerably if the bank is surfaced to readers before publication — please confirm whether that is planned for version 1.

personas.summary: This chapter is unusually text-forward, and that works strongly in its favor: every nugget's chemistry (carbonyl polarization, the addition mechanism, acetal/imine/enamine formation, 1,2 vs 1,4 selectivity, IR/NMR values) is carried by prose rather than by an unlabeled figure, all 13 assets are simple molecule renders with chemically substantive alt text that the reader also prints visibly as 'Described as: …', and every question stimulus and option is plain text or a condensed formula — no color, motion, hover, or spatial coding carries meaning anywhere in the package. I ran the repository's own answer-leak guard over all 36 compiled questions and it flagged nothing, and my manual read of every accessible_description found none that hands over the answer. Two real barriers remain. First, the four structure_scaffold questions (draw the cyanohydrin, draw the Wittig alkene, plus their v2 variants) are required response-by-drawing on the Ketcher canvas; the platform itself records keyboard_complete=False for that type and declares a nonvisual_response_mode ('structured_molecule_entry') that has no implementation anywhere in the student frontend — a learner who cannot use a fine-pointer canvas simply cannot answer them, even though the grader already accepts a SMILES string. Second, the carefully authored accessible_description on all 36 questions appears to be metadata that no student-facing renderer actually reads, so the non-visual task framing the author wrote may never reach a screen-reader user. Beyond those, the issues are modest: a heading-level skip in the reader, an undescribed acetal structure in the error-repair item, unlabeled per-option structures, and an alt text that numbers but does not name the alpha/beta carbons the conjugate-addition concept depends on.

location.anchor_text: Draw the alkene formed when cyclohexanone reacts with methylenetriphenylphosphorane

findings.observation: Four required questions — ch19-draw-cyanohydrin, ch19-draw-cyanohydrin-v2, ch19-draw-wittig-product, ch19-draw-wittig-product-v2 — are question_type structure_scaffold with student_config [redacted]. Answering means drawing a structure in the Ketcher canvas. The platform's own type manifest at [internal source reference — not in this repo] records keyboard_complete=False and declares nonvisual_response_mode="structured_molecule_entry", but that response mode appears nowhere in the frontend: the two student surfaces for this type ([internal source reference — not in this repo] and [internal source reference — not in this repo]) offer only a same-origin generator iframe plus a 'Submit canvas structure' button, with no SMILES or text-entry field. There is therefore no implemented alternative response path in this chapter's delivery.
findings.learner_impact: A student who is blind, has low vision, uses a screen reader, or cannot use a mouse/trackpad-style pointing device cannot complete four of this chapter's questions at all — including the only production-style assessment of cyanohydrin formation and the only production-style assessment of the Wittig product. They are excluded from graded work their sighted, pointer-using classmates complete, on two concepts (hydration-and-cyanohydrins, wittig-reaction) where drawing the product is the stated task.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json question_sets: slugs ch19-draw-cyanohydrin / -v2 / ch19-draw-wittig-product / -v2, question_type 'structure_scaffold', student_config [redacted], answer_key [redacted] etc. compiled/question-set.json counts.by_type shows structure_scaffold: 4. [internal source reference — not in this repo]: keyboard_complete=False. [internal source reference — not in this repo] contains only onSubmit("canvas_structure").
findings.recommended_outcome: These four items need a response path that does not require drawing on a pointer-driven canvas — the answer key is already a SMILES string and STRUCTURE_GRADER already grades chemical graphs, so an equivalent non-drawing way to submit the same chemical answer (or an equivalent alternate task assessing the same objective) must exist before the chapter is assigned as graded work.

location.anchor_text: Sort six named carbonyl compounds into two families based on the substitution at the carbonyl carbon.

findings.observation: All 36 questions carry a well-written accessibility_bundle.accessible_description, and it survives compilation into compiled/question-set.json and into the backend LMS envelope ([internal source reference — not in this repo] sets accessibilityBundle). But no general student renderer reads it: searching the frontend for accessible_description / accessibilityDescription / accessibilityBundle finds only MolecularGeometryRenderer (its own responseConfig key), ReactionCoordinateQuestionRenderer (reads accessibilityBundle.description, a different key), and the internal QuestionTypeDemoPage. The delivery panels used for a chapter question set — [internal source reference — not in this repo] and [internal source reference — not in this repo] — render only the prompt. None of this chapter's 11 question types is one of the two renderers that read an accessibility bundle.

location.anchor_text: The carbonyl group, and how aldehydes and ketones are named

With 17 molecule figures and 11 sections, this is the primary navigation scaffold for the chapter.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo]: Heading as="h1" (chapter), Heading as="h2" (section); [internal source reference — not in this repo]: Heading as="h4" for molecule, video, link, and reaction-coordinate blocks.

findings.observation: This error_repair item ships a structural stimulus, student_config.molecule_smiles = 'C1CCC2(CC1)OCCO2' (the cyclohexanone ethylene acetal), but its accessible_description ('Diagnose and repair a claim about how an acetal protecting group is removed after a Grignard addition') never describes that structure. location.anchor_text: 4-Methyl-2-pentanone

findings.observation: Several questions attach per-option structures — ch19-iupac-name and ch19-iupac-name-v2 options carry structure_smiles, and both rank_order items give each card a structure_smiles — but none of these structures has an authored accessible name, and [internal source reference — not in this repo] only renders an option's imageUrl (alt={option.text}), ignoring structure_smiles entirely. findings.learner_impact: Today the options are effectively text-only, which is accessible; the risk is asymmetric access if a surface begins rendering these structures, since a screen-reader user would get only the option name while a sighted user gets name plus picture — and in the IUPAC item the picture would actively mislead by showing two different names over one structure.

findings.observation: The only figure supporting the conjugate-addition concept is described as 'a four-carbon chain in which carbon 2 forms a double bond to oxygen (the ketone) and carbons 3 and 4 form a carbon–carbon double bond conjugated with it'. The alt text uses locants only and never maps C3 to the beta position.
findings.learner_impact: A learner working entirely from the description has to derive the locant-to-alpha/beta mapping themselves at the moment the concept is introduced, adding a translation step to the chapter's single hardest regiochemical distinction. The prose does define beta as 'two atoms away', so this is recoverable, not blocking.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json asset mol-methyl-vinyl-ketone accessibility.alt_text; nugget-conjugate-addition prose 'positive character appearing at two carbons: the carbonyl carbon and the beta carbon, two atoms away'.
findings.recommended_outcome: The description of the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone needs to name the alpha and beta carbons in the same vocabulary the concept and its question use, so the non-visual reader gets the labeling directly rather than deriving it.

location.anchor_text: One mechanism, many reactions: nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl

findings.observation: Three video blocks are compiled into the reader (nugget-nucleophilic-addition, nugget-acetals, nugget-wittig) with url: "" and is_hidden: true; [internal source reference — not in this repo] returns null for hidden blocks, so students currently see nothing — the videos are deferred at authoring. The compiled block would otherwise render a 'Watch →' link to an empty route. The video_briefs each record the caption/narration/transcript requirement as a production note only; nothing in the package yet holds the caption or transcript content.
findings.learner_impact: No present barrier — the mechanism content is carried in prose, which is fully accessible. The risk is future: if these blocks are unhidden when the videos are produced, three mechanism animations enter the chapter and the deaf/hard-of-hearing and non-visual equivalents (captions, descriptive narration of electron flow, transcript, and pause/step controls) would have to already exist, and a broken empty-url link would ship in the interim.
findings.evidence: frontend/public/reader/topic-chapters/aldehydes-and-ketones.json blocks blk-r8gcfq5b, blk-ijjski5m, blk-pmnwmeje: {"url": "", "is_external": false, "is_hidden": true}; topic.package.json video_briefs[*].production_note 'Production requirement recorded: include a closed-caption track and narration that names every meaningful visual change … plus a text transcript.'

strengths: Every question stimulus and every answer option in all 36 questions is plain text or a condensed formula (e.g. 'Trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral), Cl₃CCHO', 'Lithium dimethylcuprate, (CH₃)₂CuLi') — no item requires reading an unlabeled structure to choose an answer.

I ran the repository's own guard ([internal source reference — not in this repo]::find_accessibility_leaks) over all 36 compiled questions: zero leaks. Manual review agrees — the accessible descriptions consistently state the task ('determining which atoms end up on the former carbonyl carbon is part of the task') without the answer.

All 13 molecule assets carry alt text that describes chemically relevant connectivity rather than naming the image (e.g. the cyclic acetal: 'a six-membered carbon ring sharing one carbon with a five-membered ring that contains two oxygen atoms; the shared carbon is bonded to both oxygens and bears no hydroxyl or carbonyl group'), and the reader prints it visibly as 'Described as: …' beneath every structure, benefiting low-vision and cognitive-access users too.

The drag-flavored question types this chapter uses are all implemented as keyboard-complete controls, not drag-and-drop: CategorizeRenderer is one labeled Select per item with aria-label 'Category for X', MatchingRenderer likewise, MechanismCardSortRenderer provides 'Move up'/'Move down' buttons with position-announcing labels, and ComparisonMatrixRenderer is a semantic table of keyboard-reachable selects.
Nothing in the chapter uses color, motion, spatial position, or hover as the sole carrier of meaning; there are no animations, no interactive spectra, and no color-coded diagrams to fail on.
All 76 hints across the question set are text hints — no hint requires seeing a highlight, projection label, or animation — and every nugget's practice_check is answerable purely in prose.

The 11 nuggets carry the mechanism and spectroscopy content in full sentences with explicit numbers (1730/1715/1690 cm⁻¹, 9–10 ppm, 206 ppm), and no prose sentence points at a figure with 'as shown', 'below', or a color word — so nothing in the reading depends on a visual the learner may not receive.
